projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Pound: I am sorry to trouble you but if you are assistant-editor of
This Quarter
as I understand could you ask the Italian printer to set up my piece before the rest of the review. I have very little time as I have to go back to Paris to undergo another operation. This suspense makes me nervous and I want a few weeks’ complete rest after I have corrected the proofs. These should be sent to Miss Beach , registered, as soon as possible. The text is difficult too, especially for a foreign printer. I wrote to Mr Walsh who said he would arrange it if he could but he is not on the spot. This is my excuse for troubling you .
I hope Mrs Pound and yourself are well. We have a flat of our own in Paris: 2 Square Robiac, 192 rue de Grenelle and if I had my sight all would be well enough. It is very trying on one’s nerves.
This is a splendid place here but unfortunately we are caught in a rainy spell.

div.note: JJ was between eye operations, and his ophthalmologist, Dr. Louis Borsch, suggested that he leave Paris for a holiday before his next surgery, at that time planned for September 1925. JJ and family left for Fécamp in Normandy, then went to Rouen and, driven by rainy weather, proceeded down to Arcachon, a seaside resort on the Atlantic coast southwest of Bordeaux, with a climate favorable for invalids (Ellmann, JJ 572-73). JJ considered Arcachon “a very nice place” (LIII 126), and spent nearly a month there at the Régina Palace Hotel & d’Angleterre, which was advertised as having “all modern comforts. Exceptionally well situated in a pine forest, three minutes from the beach. Billiard room. Electricity. Central heating. Elevator. Rooms with bath. Hot and cold running water in all rooms. … English spoken” (Rouen and its Vicinity [Paris: Hachette, 1920], 70 [translated from French]). At the time, JJ was planning and working on the last watch of Shaun, the section of “Work in Progress” that would later be published as pages 555-90 of Finnegans Wake (1939). He returned to Paris on 5 September.

This Quarter was a review devoted to experimental literature, art, and music, edited by the American poet Ernest Walsh (1895-1926) and the Scottish suffragist Ethel Moorhead (1869-1955), who helped finance Walsh and the magazine. They produced the first issue from Paris, then moved their headquarters to Milan so that Walsh, who suffered from tuberculosis, could benefit from the warmer climate. After his death, Moorhead produced the third and fourth numbers from Monte Carlo. Later numbers were edited by Edward W. Titus (1870-1952), but the magazine became insolvent and ceased publication in 1932. The first issue of This Quarter (Spring 1925, octavo, 270 pages) was dedicated to “Ezra Pound who by his creative work, his editorship of several magazines, his helpful friendship for young and unknown artists, his many and untiring efforts to win better appreciation of what is first-rate in art, comes first to our mind as meriting the gratitude of this generation.” At Walsh’s request, JJ wrote a testimonial to Pound’s “friendly help, encouragement and generous interest in everything that I have written” (LIII 117), which was printed, along with an encomium by Ernest Hemingway, in the first issue. This Quarter printed three of Pound’s cantos (Cantos 17-19) in its second number (Autumn-Winter 1925-1926), for which Pound was paid £40. However, Pound offended Moorhead by his indifference to Walsh’s poetry, and she withdrew the dedication in the third issue. Although Pound had been offering his usual informal advice to This Quarter, he had no official editorial role.

A portion of JJ’s “Work in Progress” was published in This Quarter (Milan), vol. 1, no. 2 (Autumn-Winter 1925-1926): 108-123. This portion would become what is known as the Shem chapter, Book I, Chapter 7, of Finnegans Wake (1939), pages 169-95. In the dream-distorted world of the Wake, Shem the Penman and his brother Shaun are the sons of HCE and his wife ALP. A third child is their daughter, Issy. In the Shem chapter, Shaun describes Shem disparagingly as “a sham and a low sham” and charges him with, among other offenses, producing “piously forged palimpsests … from his pelagiarist pen” (FW 170, 182). Shem, who is a writer figure, bears a resemblance to the expatriate JJ, who, like Shem, “would far sooner muddle through the hash of lentils in Europe than meddle with Irrland’s split little pea” (FW 171). In addition to This Quarter, JJ was publishing portions of “Work in Progress” in various other periodicals around this time: Transatlantic Review, Criterion, and Le Navire d’Argent.

Dr. Louis Borsch operated on JJ’s left eye – JJ’s seventh surgery – in mid-April 1925 in Paris. JJ remained in the clinic for ten days. Borsch was planning to operate again in September, but surgery was postponed until December 1925, when JJ underwent two operations, his eighth and ninth (Ellmann, JJ 570, 572-73).

Sylvia Beach acted as a steward and clearing house for JJ’s publishing, financial, and personal needs, and was assisting him with correcting proofs for various portions of “Work in Progress” that were appearing in reviews (see James Joyce’s Letters to Sylvia Beach, 1921-1940, ed. Melissa Banta and Oscar Silverman [Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1987], 56-89).
Ernest Walsh edited This Quarter with Ethel Moorhead (see note 2 above).

Editorial headquarters for This Quarter had moved from Paris to Milan (see note 2 above). Since early 1925, Pound and his wife Dorothy, née Shakespear (1886-1973), had been living in a top-floor apartment at 12 via Marsala in the northern Italian town of Rapallo, about 15 miles from Genoa and just over 100 miles from Milan. For more details of Pound’s move from Paris to Italy, see JJ to Pound, 31 December 1924, notes.

Pound’s reply to this letter, if any, has not come to light, but he published a letter in the Paris edition of the Chicago Tribune in early September 1925, announcing his unavailability as a factotum for the literary world: “I have no editorial connection with any current periodical; and … I am not a receiving station for manuscript, typescript, drawings, photographs or other paraphernalia, accompanied or unaccompanied by return postage (French, Guatemalian, or Etats Unisien)” (Chicago Tribune [Paris] [3 September 1925]: 4). JJ wrote Harriet Shaw Weaver on 10 October 1925 that, in addition to Pound’s Tribune letter, “[t]here have been other allusions since, all at the same time,” creating “a very curious atmosphere about here since I came back [from holiday]” (LI 234). JJ had come to suspect that Pound was hostile to him and his post-Ulysses literary experiments.

In early June 1925, JJ and family moved from 8 avenue Charles Floquet, near the Eiffel Tower, to a flat about a mile away at 2 Square Robiac, off 192 rue de Grenelle. He remained there “longer than at any other of his Paris addresses, until April 30, 1931” (Ellmann, JJ 571).
